blocks.text: **Searching** means finding where a value is — or proving it isn't there. Looking up a contact, checking whether a username is taken, finding the first log line after midnight: all searches. There are two basic ways to do it, and the gap between them is one of the biggest in all of computing.

blocks.alt: Finding 23 in the sorted array 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91. Linear search checks 2, 5, 8, 12, 16 and then 23: six checks. Binary search checks the middle, 16, then 56, then 23: three checks. For a billion values linear search may need a billion checks and binary search about 30.

items: **Linear search** checks the values one by one from the start. It works on **any** data — unsorted, a linked list, a stream — and costs **O(n)**.

**Binary search** needs the data **sorted**. It checks the middle value: if the target is bigger, the whole left half can be thrown away; if smaller, the right half. Every check halves what's left, so it costs **O(log n)** — about 30 checks for a billion values.

blocks.text: Other structures are built for searching too: a **hash table** finds a key in O(1) on average (Hashing course), a **binary search tree** in O(log n) while staying sorted as values come and go (Binary Search Tree course), and **BFS and DFS** search graphs (Graph course). This course is about searching arrays and ranges — and above all, binary search.
The real power of binary search

Binary search isn't only for finding a number in a sorted array. It works on **any yes/no question whose answer flips once**: false, false, …, false, true, true, …, true. Binary search finds the flip point in O(log n) checks. That one idea solves a surprising range of interview problems:

items: **Positions in sorted data** — the first value at least 7, the last 5, where to insert 4.
**Hidden order** — the first bad version of a program, the peak of a mountain, the smallest value of a rotated array.
**Answers in a range** — the smallest eating speed that finishes in time, the smallest ship that carries everything in d days. You don't search an array at all: you search the **possible answers**.
**Target** — the value (or condition) being searched for.
**Search space** — the indexes or answers still possible, usually `low..high`. Each step must shrink it.
**mid** — the middle of the search space, the one value checked each step.
**Invariant** — a fact that stays true every step, like "if the target exists, it's between low and high". It's how you write binary search without off-by-one bugs.
**Monotonic** — a condition that, once true, stays true (or once false, stays false). Binary search needs one.
**Lower bound / upper bound** — the first index with a value **at least** the target / **greater than** the target.

blocks.text: Every language has a built-in linear search. Use it for unsorted data:
For **sorted** data, most languages also ship a binary search — though JavaScript doesn't, and interviews usually ask you to write one anyway:

blocks.code:
Python      bisect.bisect_left(nums, target)                  # first index with nums[i] >= target
            bisect.bisect_right(nums, target)                 # first index with nums[i] > target
Java        Arrays.binarySearch(nums, target)                 # an index of target, or -(insert position) - 1
C++         lower_bound(nums.begin(), nums.end(), target)     # first value >= target
            binary_search(nums.begin(), nums.end(), target)   # true or false
JavaScript  (none built in: write it yourself)

blocks.text: The rest of this introduction builds these from scratch: linear search, binary search, the lower and upper bound templates, and binary search on the answer — each one drawn, simulated and timed.

items: **Linear search** works on anything and costs **O(n)**.
**Binary search** needs sorted data — or any condition that flips once — and costs **O(log n)**.
Binary search can search **answers**, not just arrays: that's the trick behind many hard-looking problems.
Write binary search around an **invariant** to avoid off-by-one bugs.
